translations.text: Chapter 1. When the king of the Chaldeans took the Israelites captive, God spoke to Jeremiah and said to him, “Jeremiah, my chosen one, rise and leave this city, you and Baruch, for I am about to destroy it because of the many sins of those who live in it.
For your prayer is like a strong pillar in the middle of the city and like an adamant wall around it. Now rise, go, and leave before the army of the Chaldeans comes and surrounds the city.”
Jeremiah spoke, saying, “I beg you, my Lord, allow your servant to speak before you.” God said to him, “Speak, Jeremiah, my chosen one.”
Jeremiah spoke and said, “Lord, who holds all things, will you hand this chosen city over to the Chaldeans, so that the king may boast with his people and say, ‘I have conquered the city of God’?
Far be it, Lord! If this is your will, destroy it with your own hand.”
The Lord said to Jeremiah, “Because you are my chosen one, rise and leave, you and Baruch, for I am about to destroy it because of the sins of those who live in it.
Neither the king nor his army can enter the city unless I first go ahead and open its gates. Now rise, go to Baruch, and tell him this.
Rise when it is the sixth hour of the night and come to the city wall, and I will show you. Unless I first begin destroying the city, they cannot enter it.”
After saying this, the Lord departed from Jeremiah.
Chapter 2. Then Jeremiah tore his clothes, put dust on his head, and entered the temple.
When Baruch saw Jeremiah with his head covered in earth and his clothes torn, he cried out loudly, saying, “My father Jeremiah, what has happened to you? What sin have the people committed?”
For whenever the people sinned, Jeremiah would grieve, put dust on his head, and pray for the people until their transgression was forgiven.
Baruch asked him, “My father Jeremiah, what has happened to you, and what has happened to the people?”

Jeremiah said to him, “Take care that we tear not our clothes but our hearts. Let us not put water into bowls, so that we may weep freely until we fill them with tears, for from now on no mercy will be shown to this people.”
Baruch said, “My father Jeremiah, what has happened to you?” Jeremiah said to him, “God is handing the city over to the king of the Chaldeans, for he will cruelly take the people captive.”
When Baruch heard all this, he tore his clothes and said, “My father Jeremiah, what message have they sent you?”
Jeremiah said to him, “Stay with me until the sixth hour of the night, so that you may know that the message is true.” They remained in the temple, weeping.
Chapter 3. When the sixth hour of the night came, at which the Lord had told Jeremiah to go out with Baruch, they came to the city wall and stayed there waiting.
There was a sound of a horn, and angels came out of heaven, carrying flaming torches in their hands, and stood at the city wall.
Then Jeremiah and Baruch wept, saying, “Now we know that the message is true.”
Jeremiah pleaded with the angels, saying, “I beg you, do not destroy the whole city until I ask God one thing.”
The Lord spoke to the angels, saying, “Do not destroy the city until I speak with Jeremiah, my chosen one.”
Then Jeremiah spoke, saying, “I beg you, my Lord, allow me to speak with you.” He said to him, “Speak whatever you wish, Jeremiah, my chosen one.”
Jeremiah said to him, “Look, my Lord, now we know that you are handing the city over to its enemies and that the people of Babylon will take it.
What do you wish me to do with the holy [?] that we use in our secret service? What do you wish me to do with them?”

The Lord said to him, “Take them and entrust them to the earth and to the temple, saying, ‘You also, earth, hear the voice of your Creator, who created you by the power of the waters and sealed you with seven seals. Receive your beauty and guard the treasures that adorn you until the coming of the Beloved.’”
Jeremiah spoke and said, “I beg you, my Lord, show me what I should do for Abimelech the Ethiopian, who has done so much to protect the people and me, your servant Jeremiah,
more than all the people of the city. He brought me out of the muddy pit. Do not let him see the city’s destruction and ruin, so that he may not grieve.”
The Lord said to Jeremiah, “Send him to Agrippa’s vineyard, along the road to the mountain, and I will shelter him until I bring the people back into the city.
But you, Jeremiah, go with the people until you reach the land of Babylon, and remain there prophesying to them until I bring them back into their city.
Leave Baruch here in Jerusalem.” The Lord told Jeremiah all this and went away from Jeremiah into heaven.

Jeremiah and Baruch entered the temple and entrusted all the vessels in their possession to the earth, as the Lord had commanded them. Immediately the earth swallowed them, and the two of them sat down and wept.
Early the next morning, Jeremiah sent Abimelech away, saying, “Take a basket and go along the mountain road to Agrippa’s vineyard,
and bring some figs for the sick among the people, for the joy of the Lord and his glory rest upon your head.” He went as Jeremiah had commanded him. Chapter 4.
Early the next morning, the army of the Chaldeans surrounded the city. A great angel blew a horn and said, “Enter, army of the Chaldeans! Look, the gates are opening for you.”
Then the king entered with his army, and they took all the people captive.

Then Jeremiah took the keys of the temple, went outside the city, and threw the keys toward the sun, saying, “To you I speak, sun! Take the keys of the house of God and guard them until the time when God asks you for them.
For our generation was not worthy to guard them, because we ourselves were found [?] in our sin.”
While Jeremiah was weeping for the people, they brought him out, forcing him along, and drove him with the people as far as Babylon.

But Baruch took dust and put it on his head. He sat down and uttered this lament, saying, “Why has Jerusalem been destroyed? It is because of the sin of the beloved people. She has been handed over to her enemy because of our sins and those of the people.

But let sinners not boast and say, ‘We were able to capture the city of God by our own strength.’ It was not by your might that you overcame her; rather, she was handed over to you because of our sins.
Our God will have mercy on us and bring us back into our city, but for you there is no life.
Blessed are our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for they departed from this world without seeing the destruction of this city.”
After saying this, he went out weeping and said, “I grieve for you, Jerusalem.” He went out of the city and lived among the tombs, and angels would come and tell him about everything. Chapter 5.

At noon Abimelech was bringing figs from the place where Jeremiah had sent him. He found a tree with thick foliage and sat in its shade to rest a little. He rested his head on the basket of figs and slept for sixty-six years without waking from his sleep.
After those days, he rose and awoke from his sleep and said, “If only I could sleep a little longer, for my head is still heavy, and I have not had enough sleep.”
He opened the basket of figs and found the figs fresh and dripping with their milky sap.

He wanted to sleep again, because his head was heavy and he had not had enough sleep. But he said, “I am afraid to sleep and slumber, lest my father Jeremiah rebuke me, for he sent me out early in the morning in a hurry.
Now I will get up and go, for the heat has grown intense, and it never lets up anywhere.”
He got up, took his basket of figs, and entered the city of Jerusalem. He did not recognize the city or his own house, and he said, “Blessed are you, Lord!” For great bewilderment had come over him.
And he said, “Is this not the city of Jerusalem? Perhaps I am mistaken, for I came by the mountain road.
“Or is it because my head is heavy, I have not had enough sleep, and my mind has become forgetful? How shall I report this matter to Jeremiah—that the city has become strange to me?”
He looked for every landmark in the city to find out whether it really was Jerusalem. He went back into the city again and searched for anyone he knew, but found no one.
And he said, “Blessed are you, Lord, for great bewilderment has fallen upon me.” He went out again, far from the city, and sat grieving, not knowing where to go.
He set down that basket of figs and said, “I will stay here until God removes this affliction from me.”
After he had sat there, he saw an elderly man coming in from the field. Abimelech said to him, “You there, old man, I am speaking to you! What city is this?” The old man told him, “It is Jerusalem.”
Abimelech said to him, “Where are Jeremiah the priest, Baruch the Levite, and all the people of this city? For I have found none of them.”
The old man said to him, “Are you not from this city? And do you only now remember Jeremiah and ask about him, after being here all these days?
“Jeremiah is in Babylon with the people, for he was taken captive and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia. He went there to prophesy to them.”

When Abimelech heard this from the old man, he said to him, “If you were not an elderly man, I would have insulted you and laughed at you. But it is not right to treat an elderly man with contempt. Otherwise, I would have said, ‘You have lost your mind!’

“As for your saying that the people were taken captive to Babylon, even if a mighty torrent from heaven had fallen upon them, there would not have been time for them to go to Babylon. Yet you say, ‘They were taken captive to Babylon!’
“As for me, my father Jeremiah sent me, and I went to Agrippa’s vineyard for a few figs to give to the sick among the people.

“I went and arrived there, took what he had ordered me to get, and returned. As I was walking, I found a tree and sat beneath it to shelter in its shade, because it was noon. Then I leaned against the basket of figs

“and slept. When I awoke, I thought I had only dozed off. I opened this basket of figs and found them dripping milky sap, just as when I had picked them. Yet here you are saying, ‘The people were taken captive to Babylon!’
“Look now, even the figs have not withered.” He opened the basket of figs for him and showed him. The old man saw that the figs were fresh and that their milky sap was dripping.

Then the old man was amazed and said to Abimelech, “You are righteous, my son, for God did not wish you to see the destruction of the city. God brought comfort upon you and kept you alive. Look, today it has been sixty-six years since the people were taken captive to Babylon.
“If you wish to know and make certain, my son, look at the fields and see how their crops have sprouted, and that it is not the season for figs.”

He understood that it was not the season for all this. Then Abimelech said in a loud voice, “I bless you, Lord my God, God of heaven and earth, the resting place of the souls of the righteous wherever they go!”
He said to the old man, “What month is this?” He told him, “It is the twelfth of the month of Nisan, which is Miyazya.”
After this, Abimelech gave the old man some of these figs and said to him, “May God guide you to the Jerusalem above.” Section 6.
Abimelech rose, went outside the city, and prayed to the Lord. And behold, an angel came and guided him to Baruch, and he found him sitting in a tomb.

When they had greeted one another, wept together, and kissed one another, he saw the figs in the basket. He raised his eyes to heaven and prayed, saying, “Great is God, who gives his righteous ones their reward!

“Be anointed, my soul, and rejoice as you speak to the fleshly body concerning the holy house [?]. Your clay will return to light, and after this the faithful one will come and bring you back into your body.

“Look to your virgin faith, and believe that you will live. Look at these figs: behold, it has been sixty-six years since they were picked, yet they have neither decayed nor rotted. Instead, their milky sap is still dripping.
“So it will be done to you, my flesh, because you kept the commandment given you by the angel of righteousness. The one who preserved the basket of figs will also preserve you by his power.”

When Baruch had said this, Abimelech answered him, “Get up; let us pray again, so that the Lord may show us the words we should write to Jeremiah in Babylon about the protection with which he sheltered me.”
Baruch prayed and said, “God the Lord is my strength, and so is the light that comes from his mouth. First I beseech you and take refuge in your goodness.
Great is your name, and no one can comprehend it. Hear the prayer of your servant, so that your will may be known in my heart, for me to carry it out and send it to your priest Jeremiah in Babylon.”
While he was praying this, an angel came and said to him, “Baruch, counselor of light, do not worry about how you yourself will send a message to Jeremiah.
For [?], at daybreak an eagle will come to you. You yourself must [?] concerning Jeremiah and write in a letter. Say this to the children of Israel:
‘Whoever is a foreigner among you must separate himself and remain alone for fifteen days. After this I will bring you into the city, says the Lord.
As for whoever has not separated himself within fifteen days, Jeremiah will enter the city from Babylon and rebuke the people of Babylon, says the Lord.’”
When the angel had said this, he departed from Baruch, and Baruch accompanied him as far as the open square. Then he brought papyrus and ink and wrote, saying, “From Baruch,
the servant of God, who writes a letter to Jeremiah in captivity in Babylon: Joy and gladness! For God does not abandon us to go out in our sorrow amid [?] and corruption.
Because of this, the Lord had mercy on our tears and remembered the ordinance he had previously established with our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

He sent his angel to me and told me these things that I am sending to you. These are the things done by the Lord, the God of Israel, who brought us out of the fiery land of Egypt: ‘Because you did not keep

all his righteous ordinances, but raised up your [?] and stiffened your necks before him, he delivered you into the furnace of Babylon, because you did not listen to my voice,’ says the Lord through the mouth of Jeremiah his servant.
‘Those who listened I will bring out of Babylon, and they will no longer be exiles from Jerusalem in Babylon.

If you wish to recognize them and examine them, test them with the water of the Jordan. Whoever does not listen will be recognized by the sign of this sign, which makes the seal greater [?].’ Chapter 7.

After writing this, Baruch got up and came out of the tomb. The eagle said to him, “Greetings, Baruch, steward of the faith!” Baruch said to it, “You speak because you are chosen above all the birds of heaven.
You are known by the brightness of your eyes. Now tell me why you are staying here.” The eagle said to him, “I was sent here so that you might send me with whatever message you wish.”
Baruch said to it, “Can you deliver these words to Jeremiah in Babylon?” The eagle said to him, “This is why I was sent.”
Baruch took the letter and fifteen figs from the basket of figs that Abimelech had brought, and tied them around the eagle’s neck.
He said to it, “To you I speak, eagle, king of all the birds: Go in peace and safety, and bring us news.
Do not be like the raven that Noah sent out, which refused to return to him again. Instead, be like the dove that brought word back to Noah three times.
Likewise, take these good words to Jeremiah and to the Israelites who are with him, so that it may go well with you. Carry this joy to the people chosen by God.

Even if all the birds and all the enemies of righteousness surround you, wanting to kill you, press on, and the Lord will give you strength. Do not turn to the right or to the left, but go straight, like an arrow, in the strength of God.”

When Baruch had said this, the eagle flew off with the letter and went to Babylon. It landed on a pillar outside the city, in a deserted place, and waited there until Jeremiah and the other people should pass by.
They passed that way to bury a man who had died, for Jeremiah had asked Nebuchadnezzar, “Give me some land where I may bury those of my people who die,” and he had given it to him.

As they walked along, weeping over the dead man, they came before the eagle. The eagle cried out in a loud voice and said, “To you I speak, Jeremiah, chosen one of God! Go and gather all the people, and let them come here to hear the good news I have brought.”
When he heard this, he praised God. Then he gathered all the people, their wives, and their children, and they came to where the eagle was.
The eagle came down to the corpse and touched it, and it came to life. He did this so that they would believe, and all the people marveled at what had happened.
They said, “Truly, this is the God who appeared to our fathers in the wilderness with Moses. He took the form of an eagle and appeared to us as a great eagle.”
The eagle said to Jeremiah, “Come and listen to this letter, and read it to the people.” And he read it to them.
When the people heard it, they all wept together and put dust on their heads. They said to Jeremiah, “Save us! What must we do to return to our city?”
Jeremiah stood up and said to them, “Do everything that you heard in the letter, and he will bring you back to your city.”

Jeremiah wrote a letter to Baruch, saying: “My beloved son, do not grow weary of prayer as you plead with God for us, so that he may guide us on our journey until we depart by the command of this sinful king.
“But you have found righteousness before God, who did not allow you to come with us, so that you would not see the evil being done to the people in Babylon.

“It is like a father who has only one child, and that child is handed over to be condemned. Those who are with his father to comfort him cover their faces so that they will not see his father brought low by grief.
“In the same way, God had mercy on you and did not allow you to come to Babylon, so that you would not see the suffering of the people.

“For from the day we arrived in this city until today, we have had no relief from sorrow—sixty-six years today. As we search, we find some of the people hung up by King Nebuchadnezzar, weeping and saying, ‘Have mercy on us, god Zor!’
“When I heard these words, I grieved and wept, because those who were hung up were calling upon another god and saying, ‘Have mercy on us!’
“I also remember the festival we celebrated in Jerusalem before we were taken captive. When I remember it, I return to my house in anguish and tears.
“Now, you and Abimelech, plead with our God where you are on behalf of the people, so that they may listen to my voice and the words of my mouth and leave Persia.

“And now I tell you: throughout all the days we have lived here, they have seized us, saying, ‘Sing us a new song from the songs of Zion, a song of your God.’ But we say to them, ‘How can we sing for you while we are in a foreign land?’”
After Jeremiah had written this, he tied his letter around the eagle’s neck and said to it, “Go in peace, and may the Lord protect you.”
The eagle departed and flew away, carrying the letter to Baruch. Baruch took the letter and read it, and he wept when he heard of the people’s pain and suffering.
Jeremiah took those figs and gave them to the sick among the people. He remained there, teaching them not to follow the practices of the people of Babylon. Section 8.

When the day came for God to bring the people out of Babylon, the Lord said to Jeremiah, “Rise, you and your people, and come to the Jordan. Tell the people, ‘The Lord wishes to cover over the deeds of the people of Babylon.

“‘As for the men among you who have married women, and the women who have married men from among them, we will test them.’ Bring those who listen to you back to Jerusalem, but do not allow those who do not listen to you to enter it.”
Jeremiah read all this to them and brought them to the Jordan to test them.

While he was telling them these words that the Lord had spoken to him, those who had married doubted and refused to listen to Jeremiah. Some said to him, “We will never leave our wives. We will take them with us to our city.”
They crossed the Jordan and reached Jerusalem. Jeremiah, Baruch, and Abimelech stood there, saying, “No man who has married a woman from Babylon may enter our city.”
Those who had married women said to their companions, “Get up! Let us return to Babylon.” So they went away and returned.
When the people of Babylon saw them, they came out to refuse them entry. They would not allow them to enter Babylon, saying, “You hated us first, and you left in secret.”
from us. Therefore, do not enter our city, for we have sworn by the name of our God that we will not receive you or your daughters, because you left us secretly.

When they heard this, they returned to Jerusalem and built themselves cities in the districts around Jerusalem. They named that city Samaria. Jeremiah sent word to them, saying, “Repent and wait. The angel of righteousness will come and bring you back to your spacious dwelling place.”
Chapter 9. They remained there, rejoicing and offering sacrifices for the people for seven days. On the tenth day after this happened, Jeremiah offered a sacrifice by himself.
Jeremiah prayed, saying, “Holy, holy, holy! You are a sweet fragrance to humanity and the true light that shines for me until I come before you.
I implore you on behalf of your people, and I ask you by the harmonious voice of the seraphim and by the fragrance of the cherubim’s incense.
I ask you—yes, Michael the singer is the angel of righteousness who opens the gates of righteousness until they enter them. I implore you, Lord of all and Lord
who holds everything and created everything, who reveals himself and was not begotten, who completed everything. All creation is hidden with him before it is secretly brought into being.”
He prayed this, and when he had finished his prayer, Jeremiah stood in the temple, with Baruch and Abimelech beside him. Jeremiah became like a man whose soul had departed from him.
Then Baruch and Abimelech fell down and cried out loudly, saying, “Woe to us! Our father Jeremiah, the priest of God, has departed from us!”
When the people heard this, they ran to him and found Jeremiah fallen down and dead. They wept, tore their clothes, put dust on their heads, and wept bitterly.
After they had prepared to bury him, a voice came, saying, “Do not wrap him for burial. He is alive, and his soul will return to his body again.”
When they heard this voice, they did not wrap him for burial. Instead, they remained around him, keeping watch over him for three days until his soul returned to his body.

A voice arose among them all and said, “Praise him with one voice! Praise God! All of you, praise the Messiah, the Son of God, who will awaken you and judge you: Jesus, the Son of God, the light of the whole world, the lamp that does not go out, and the life of faith.
After this there will be three hundred and three weeks of days until his coming to earth. The tree of life that is in Paradise and was not planted
will cause all the trees that bear fruit, and the dry trees, to come to him. He will make them bear fruit and sprout, and their fruit will remain with the angels.

And concerning the planting of trees, so that they may flourish and [?], we will give [?] in the morning to Iyor, so that their roots do not dry up like a plant whose root has not taken hold of the ground.
They will make what is red in color white as wool. Sweet water will become bitter, and bitter water will become sweet, with great joy.
And God’s joys will be for the islands, so that they may bear fruit through the word of his mouth, his own Son.

He himself will enter the world and choose twelve apostles for himself, so that what I saw may appear to them in splendor: the one sent from his Father, who comes into the world. He will go to the Mount of Olives and satisfy the hungry soul.”
In this way Jeremiah spoke about the Son of God and how he would come into the world.
When the people heard this, they became angry about it and said, “These are the words of Isaiah son of Amoz, who says, ‘I have seen God, the Son of God.’
Now get up! Let us do to him what we did to Isaiah.” But some of them said, “No! Instead, let us stone him.”

Baruch and Abimelech cried out to them, saying, “Do not kill him with this death!” Baruch and Abimelech grieved over Jeremiah. And they would not let him tell them any more of the hidden things he had seen.
Jeremiah said to them, “Be quiet! Do not weep, for they cannot kill me until I have told you everything I saw.
Now bring me a stone.” They brought him a stone, and he set it up and said, “Everlasting light, make this stone take on the appearance of a human being.”
Then a stone took on Jeremiah’s appearance and resembled him. They began stoning the stone, thinking it was Jeremiah himself.
Jeremiah told Baruch and Abimelech all the hidden things he had seen. After he had finished telling them, he went and stood among the people, wishing to complete his ministry.
Then that stone cried out to them, saying, “You foolish children of Israel! Why are you stoning me, thinking I am Jeremiah himself? Look, Jeremiah is standing among you!”

When they saw him, they ran with many stones and completed their lawless deed. They buried him, took that stone, and placed it in his tomb. They made it like a door and wrote on it, saying, “Look, this is Jeremiah’s helper.”
Chapter 4. The next morning, the army of the Chaldeans surrounded the city. A mighty angel blew a horn and said, “Enter, army of the Chaldeans! Look, the gates are being opened for you.”
Then the king entered with his army, and they took all the people captive.

Then Jeremiah took the keys of the temple, went outside the city, and threw these keys toward the sun, saying, “To you I speak, sun! Take the keys of the house of God and guard them until the time when the Lord asks you for them.
For our generation was not worthy to guard it, because we were found embracing our sin.”
While Jeremiah was weeping for the people, they brought him out, driving him along, and took him with the people as far as Babylon.

But Baruch took dust and put it on his head. He sat down and uttered this lament, saying, “Why was Jerusalem laid waste, if not because of the sin of the beloved people? She was handed over to her enemy because of our sin and that of the people.

But let sinners not boast or say, ‘We were able to take the city of God by our own power.’ It was not through your strength that you overcame her; rather, she was handed over to you because of our sin.
Our God will have mercy on us and bring us back to our city, but for you there is no life.
Blessed are our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because they departed from this world and did not see the destruction of this city.”
After saying this, he went out weeping and said, “I grieve for you, Jerusalem.” He left the city and stayed in a tomb, and angels would come and tell him about everything.

Chapter 5. Abimelech was bringing figs at noon from the place where Jeremiah had sent him. He found a thickly shaded tree and sat down in its shade to rest a little. He rested his head on the basket of figs and slept for sixty-six years without waking from his sleep.
After this time, he arose and woke from his sleep. He said, “If only I could sleep a little longer, because my head is still heavy and I have not had enough sleep.”
He opened that basket of figs and found the figs fresh and dripping milky sap.

He wanted to sleep again, because his head was heavy and he had not had enough sleep. But he said, “I am afraid to sleep or doze, lest my father Jeremiah scold me, for he sent me off in a hurry this morning.
Now I will get up and go, because the heat is intense and does not let up anywhere.”
He got up, took his basket of figs, and entered the city of Jerusalem. He did not recognize the city or his own house. He said, “Blessed are you, Lord,” for great bewilderment had come upon him.
He said, “Is this not the city of Jerusalem? [?] I must have lost my way, because I came by the mountain road.
Or perhaps it is because my head is heavy and I have not had enough sleep, and my mind is confused. How shall I tell Jeremiah about this—that the city has become unfamiliar to me?”
He searched for all the landmarks in the city to find out whether it really was Jerusalem. He went back into the city again and looked for anyone he knew, but found no one.
He said, “Blessed are you, Lord, for great bewilderment has fallen upon me.” He went far outside the city again and sat down grieving, not knowing where to go.
He set down that basket of figs and said, “I will sit here until the Lord takes this confusion away from me.”

After this, while he was sitting there, he saw an elderly man coming in from the field. Abimelech said to him, “You there, old man, I am speaking to you: what city is this?” The old man told him, “It is Jerusalem.”
Abimelech said to him, “Where are Jeremiah the priest, Baruch the Levite, and all the people of this city? For I have found none of them.”
The old man said to him, “Are you not from this city? And do you only now remember Jeremiah and ask about him, after all these days you have lived?”
“Jeremiah is in Babylon with the people, for he was taken captive and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia. He went there to prophesy to them.”

When Abimelech heard this from the old man, he said to him, “If you were not an elderly man, I would insult you and laugh at you. But it is not right to despise people, especially an elderly man. If that were not so, I would say, ‘You have lost your senses.’

“As for your saying that the people were taken captive to Babylon, even if a great downpour from heaven had fallen upon them, there would not have been time for them to go to Babylon. Yet you say, ‘They were taken captive to Babylon.’
“As for me, my father Jeremiah sent me, and I went to Agrippa’s vineyard for a few figs, so that we could give them to the sick among the people.

“I went and arrived there, took what he had ordered me to get, and returned. As I was walking, I found a tree and sat beneath it to take shelter in its shade, because it was noon. Then I leaned against the basket of figs

“and slept. When I awoke, it seemed to me that I had only dozed. I opened this basket of figs and found them dripping milky sap, just as when I had picked them. And now you say, ‘The people have been taken captive to Babylon!’
“Look! See that even the figs have not withered.” He opened the basket of figs for him and showed him. The old man looked and saw that the figs were fresh and their milky sap was dripping.

Then the old man was amazed and said to Abimelech, “You are righteous, my son, for God did not wish to let you see the destruction of the city. God brought consolation upon you and kept you alive. Look, today it has been sixty-six years since the people were taken captive to Babylon.
“If you wish to know and be certain, my son, look at the fields and see how their crops have sprouted, and that it is not the season for figs.”

He realized that it was not the season for any of these things. Then Abimelech said in a loud voice, “I bless you, Lord my God, God of heaven and earth, the rest of the souls of the righteous in all their journeys.”
He said to the old man, “What month is this?” He told him, “It is the twelfth of the month of Nisan, which is Miyazya.”
After this, Abimelech gave the old man some of these figs and said to him, “May God guide you to the Jerusalem above.”
Section 6. Abimelech got up, went outside the city, and prayed to the Lord. And behold, an angel came and led him to Baruch, whom he found sitting in a tomb.

They greeted one another, wept together, and kissed one another. When he saw the figs in his basket, he lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed, saying, “Great is God, who gives his righteous people their reward!
“Rejoice, my soul, and be glad as you speak to the body of flesh, the holy house: [?] your clay will return to light. After this the faithful one will come and bring you back into your body.

“Look to your virginity of faith, and believe, so that you may live. Look at these figs: behold, it has been sixty-six years since they were picked, yet they have neither decayed nor rotted, but their milky sap is still dripping.
“So will it be done to you, my flesh, because you kept the command given to you by the angel of righteousness. He who preserved the basket of figs will also preserve you by his power.”

When Baruch had said this, Abimelech answered him, “Get up; let us pray again, so that the Lord may show us the words we should write to Jeremiah in Babylon about the protection with which he covered me.”
Baruch prayed and said, “God the Lord is my strength, and the light that comes from his mouth. First I beseech you and appeal to your goodness.
“Great is your name, and no one can comprehend it. Hear your servant’s prayer, so that your will may be known in my heart, that I may do it and send word to your priest Jeremiah in Babylon.”
While he was praying this, an angel came and said to him, “Baruch, counselor of light, do not worry about how you will send word to Jeremiah.
“Tomorrow, at daybreak, an eagle will come to you. You yourself consider the matter of Jeremiah, write in a scroll, and speak as follows to the children of Israel:”
Let whoever is a foreigner among you be separated and remain alone for fifteen days. After this I will bring you into the city, says the Lord.
As for anyone who has not separated from Babylon within fifteen days, Jeremiah shall enter the city and rebuke the people of Babylon, says the Lord.
After saying this, the angel departed from Baruch, and Baruch accompanied him as far as the courtyard. Then he brought paper and ink and wrote as follows on behalf of Baruch:
The servant of God writes a letter to Jeremiah in captivity in Babylon: Joy and gladness! For God will not leave us to depart in sorrow, in [?] defilement and corruption.
For this reason the Lord had mercy on our tears and remembered the covenant he had previously made with our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He sent his angel to me and told me these things that I have sent to you. These are the deeds of the Lord, the God of Israel, who brought us out of the fiery land of Egypt. Because you did not keep

all his righteous ordinances, but exalted your [?] and stiffened your necks before him, he handed you over to the furnace of Babylon. For you did not listen to my voice, says the Lord through the mouth of Jeremiah his servant.
Those who listened I will bring out of Babylon, and they shall no longer be exiles from Jerusalem in Babylon.
If you wish to recognize them and test them, test them with the water of the Jordan. Whoever does not listen will be recognized by this sign, a sign that magnifies the seal.
Chapter 7. After writing these things, Baruch rose and came out of the tomb.
The eagle said to him, “Greetings, Baruch, guardian of the faith!” Baruch said to it, “You are chosen from among all the birds of heaven, for you speak.
You are recognizable by the brightness of your eyes. Now tell me why you are staying here.” The eagle said to him, “I was sent here so that you might send me with whatever message you wish.”
Baruch said to it, “Can you deliver these words to Jeremiah in Babylon?” The eagle said to him, “For this purpose I was sent.”
Baruch took the letter and fifteen figs from the basket of figs that Abimelech had brought, and tied them around the eagle’s neck.
He said to it, “I say to you, eagle, king of all the birds: Go in peace and safety, and bring us news.
Do not be like the raven that Noah sent out, which refused to return to him again. Instead, be like the dove that brought word back to Noah the third time.
Likewise, carry these good words to Jeremiah and the Israelites who are with him, so that it may go well with you. Carry this glad news to the people chosen by God.

Even if all the birds and all the enemies of righteousness surround you, seeking to kill you, press onward, and the Lord will give you strength. Do not turn either to the right or to the left, but go in the strength of God, like an arrow flying straight.”

After Baruch had said this, the eagle flew away with the letter and went to Babylon. It rested on a pillar outside the city, in a deserted place, and waited there until Jeremiah and some other people passed by.
They passed that way to bury a man who had died. For Jeremiah had asked Nebuchadnezzar, “Give me land where I may bury those of my people who die,” and he had given it to him.

As they walked along, weeping over the dead man, they came before the eagle. The eagle cried out in a loud voice, “I say to you, Jeremiah, chosen one of God: Go and gather all the people, and let them come here to hear the good news I have brought.”
When he heard this, he praised God. Immediately he gathered all the people, their wives, and their children, and they came to where the eagle was.
The eagle came down to the corpse and stepped on it, and the man came to life. It did this so that they would believe, and all the people marveled at what had happened.
They said, “Surely this is God, who appeared to our fathers in the wilderness with Moses! He has taken the form of an eagle and appeared to us as a great eagle.”
The eagle said to Jeremiah, “Come and listen to this letter, and read it to the people.” And he read it to them.
When the people heard this, they all wept together and put dust on their heads. They said to Jeremiah, “Save us! What must we do to return to our country?”
Jeremiah stood up and said to them, “Do everything you have heard in the letter, and he will bring you back to your country.”

Jeremiah wrote a letter to Baruch, saying: “My beloved son, do not grow weary of prayer, praising God on our behalf so that he may guide us on our journey until we depart by the command of this sinful king.
“You have found righteousness before God, who did not allow you to come with us, so that you would not see the evil being done to the people in Babylon.

“It is like a father who has an only son, and that son is handed over to be condemned. Those who are with his father to comfort him cover their faces so that they do not see the father brought low by grief.
“In the same way, God has had mercy on you and has not allowed you to come to Babylon, so that you would not see the people's suffering.

“For since we arrived in this country, we have had no relief from grief to this day—sixty-six years now. Every day, as we search, we find some of the people impaled by King Nebuchadnezzar, weeping and saying, ‘Have mercy on us, O god Sor!’
“When I heard these words, I grieved and wept, because those who were impaled were calling on another god and saying, ‘Have mercy on us!’
“Again I remember the festival we celebrated in Jerusalem before we were taken captive. Remembering it, I return to my house in anguish and tears.
“Now, you and Abimelech, where you are, plead with our God on behalf of the people, so that they may listen to my voice and the words of my mouth and depart from Persia.

“Now I tell you: throughout the time we have lived here, they have seized us, saying, ‘Sing us a new song from the songs of Zion, a song of your God.’ But we say to them, ‘How can we sing for you while we are in a foreign land?’”
After writing this, Jeremiah tied his letter around the eagle's neck and said to it, “Go in peace, and may the Lord watch over you.”
The eagle went off, flew away, and delivered the letter to Baruch. Baruch took the letter and read it, and he wept when he heard of the people's pain and suffering.
Jeremiah took those figs and gave them to the sick among the people. He remained there, teaching them not to follow the practices of the people of Babylon.

Chapter 8. When the day arrived on which God would bring the people out of Babylon, the Lord said to Jeremiah, “Rise, you and your people, and come to the Jordan. Tell the people, ‘The Lord wishes to cover over the deeds of the people of Babylon.

“‘As for the men among you who have married their women, and the women who have married men from among them, let us test them.’ Bring back to Jerusalem those who listen to you, but do not allow those who do not listen to you to enter it.”
Jeremiah spoke all these words to them and brought them to the Jordan to test them.

As he told them these words that the Lord had spoken to him, those who had married doubted and refused to listen to Jeremiah. Some said to him, “We will never leave our wives. We will take them with us to our country.”
They crossed the Jordan and reached Jerusalem. Jeremiah, Baruch, and Abimelech stood there, saying, “No man who has married a woman from Babylon may enter our city.”
Those who had married women said to their companions, “Get up! Let us return to Babylon.” So they went back.
When the people of Babylon saw them, they came out to refuse them entry. They would not allow them to enter Babylon, saying, “You hated us before and secretly departed
“from us. Therefore, you shall not enter our city, for we have sworn by the name of our god that we will not receive you or your daughters, because you secretly went away from us.”

When they heard this, they returned to Jerusalem and built towns for themselves in the districts around Jerusalem. They named that city Samaria. Jeremiah sent word to them, saying, “Repent and come. The angel of righteousness will come and bring you back to your spacious dwelling place.”
Chapter 9. They remained there, rejoicing and offering sacrifices for the people for seven days. On the tenth day after this happened, Jeremiah offered a sacrifice by himself.
Jeremiah prayed, saying, “Holy, holy, holy! You are a sweet fragrance to humanity and the true light that shines for me until I come before you.”
I implore you on behalf of your people, and I entreat you by the thunderous voice of the seraphim and by the fragrance of the cherubim’s incense.
I entreat you—yes, Michael, my singer, is an angel of righteousness—those who open the gates of righteousness so that they may enter them. I implore you, Lord of all and Lord,
who holds everything and created everything, who reveals himself and was not begotten, who completed everything. All creation lies hidden with him, even before things are done in secret.
Jeremiah prayed this, and when he had finished his prayer, he stood in the temple, with Baruch and Abimelech beside him. Jeremiah became like a man whose soul had departed from him.
Then Baruch and Abimelech fell down and cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Woe to us! Our father Jeremiah, the priest of God, has departed from us!”
When the people heard this, they ran to him and found Jeremiah lying dead. They wept, tore their clothes, put dust on their heads, and wept bitterly.
After they had prepared to bury him, a voice came, saying, “Do not wrap him for burial. He is alive, and his soul will return to his body again.”
When they heard this voice, they did not wrap him for burial. Instead, they remained around him, keeping watch for three days until his soul returned to his body.

A voice sounded among them all and said, “Praise him with one voice! Praise God! All of you, praise the Messiah, the Son of God, who will awaken you and judge you: Jesus, the Son of God, the light of the whole world, the lamp that never goes out, and the life of faith.
After this there will be three hundred and three weeks of days until his coming to earth. The tree of life, which is in the garden and was not planted,
will cause every fruit-bearing tree, and the dry trees, to come to him. He will make them bear fruit and sprout, and their fruit will remain with the angels.

And concerning the planting of trees, so that they may flourish and [?], let us give [?] the morning of Iyar, so that their roots do not dry up like a plant whose root has not taken hold in the ground.
They will make what is red in color white as wool. Sweet water will become bitter, and bitter water will become sweet, with great rejoicing.
And God’s joys will be for the islands, so that they may bear fruit through the word of his mouth, his Son.

He himself will enter the world and choose twelve apostles for himself, so that he may appear to them as I saw him, arrayed in splendor. He will be sent from his Father and will come into the world. He will go to the Mount of Olives and satisfy the hungry soul.”
In this way Jeremiah spoke about the Son of God and how he would come into the world.
When the people heard this, they became angry about it and said, “These are the words of Isaiah son of Amoz, who says, ‘I have seen God, the Son of God.’
Now get up! Let us do to him as we did to Isaiah.” Half of them said, “No! Instead, let us stone him.”

Baruch and Abimelech cried out to them, saying, “Do not put him to death in this way!” Baruch and Abimelech grieved over Jeremiah. Moreover, the people would not let him tell them the hidden things he had seen.
Jeremiah said to them, “Be quiet. Do not weep, for they cannot kill me until I have told you everything I have seen.
Now bring me a stone.” They brought him a stone, and he set it upright and said, “Everlasting Light, make this stone take on the appearance of a human being.”
At once the stone took on Jeremiah’s appearance and resembled him. They began stoning the stone, thinking that it was Jeremiah himself.
Jeremiah told Baruch and Abimelech all the hidden things he had seen. After he had finished telling them, he went and stood among the people, wishing to complete his appointed task.
Then that stone cried out to them and said, “You foolish children of Israel! Why are you stoning me, thinking that I am Jeremiah himself? Look, Jeremiah is standing among you!”

When they saw him, they rushed at him with many stones and completed their act of lawlessness. They buried him, took that stone, placed it in his tomb, and made it like a door. They wrote on it, saying, “Look, this is Jeremiah’s helper.”
